Installing and running¶

Priroda has no installer. You copy an executable, the basis-set files you need and, for parallel runs, the MPI launcher into a directory, write an input file, and start the program with the input and output file names as arguments.

Obtaining Priroda¶

Priroda is free of charge. The executables, the basis-set files and the helper scripts can be downloaded from the official site, https://rad.chem.msu.ru/~laikov/p_w/. Only parallel runs on Windows need more: an MPI runtime, which is not on the site (see Parallel runs on Windows). Put the executable and basis.in in a directory of your own. The main Linux executable, p, is probably statically linked (see Executables). The page is a bare file index with no documentation, license text or contact information. It holds:

  • Linux x86-64 executables (p, p4, p_d, p4_d), builds for particular clusters (p_l, p_mvs1p1, p_mvs10p, p_mvs10q), an ARM build (p_arm), a bundled mpiexec, and the molecule viewer xm;

  • Windows (Cygwin, x86-64) executables in exe64/;

  • example inputs and outputs;

  • basis-set and parameter files (basis.in, basis4.in, b2*.in, b4s*.in, 3z.bas, sbk.bas, qm.in);

  • small shell scripts: ge (append the $Energy block from an output to the input), gm (replace $molecule with the optimized geometry) and grx (join two IRC halves).

Which executable to choose is described under Executables below.

Users have also obtained the program by writing to the developer, Dimitri Laikov, by e-mail. Users reported the address dimitri_laikov@mail.ru from 2010 to 2018; earlier it was laikov@physto.se. Users note that he does not always answer quickly.

Note

The legal status is not stated on the official site. A 2009 presentation relayed on a forum said that Priroda is registered with Rospatent and distributed through the company OOO “Dimonta”. A user reported in 2018 that the developer had said, a couple of years earlier, that there was no licence agreement. Users customarily ask the developer’s permission before using the program.

The official site has hosted builds with known defects. In 2016 it carried a note that the w64/*.exe builds (an attempt at 64-bit Cygwin) had a DFT/ECP bug. If a build behaves strangely, ask the developer whether it is the right one.

The official site lists these Linux files. Dates are from the official file index (checked October 2026).

That p is statically linked is inferred from the description of p_d as “dynamically linked”. The site does not say which cluster each p_mvs* and p_l build is for.

Older distributions used other names: p6, p6_32 and p6_64 for version 6, p9, and p1 for version 11 at one site. Scripts and forum posts written for those versions use these names. This manual writes p throughout.

Some users run the Linux build under WSL on Windows.

Windows¶

The Windows build is a Cygwin build for x86-64. It is in the exe64/ directory of the official site:

File

Date

Description

p1.exe

2021-10-01

Serial executable.

p1_190306.exe

2019-03-12

Older serial build.

p_190306.exe

2019-03-12

Older parallel (MPI) build.

xm.exe

2019-03-08

Viewer.

cygwin1.dll

2021-10-01

Cygwin runtime library.

For serial runs you need only p1.exe and cygwin1.dll in the same directory. A full Cygwin installation is not required, and no administrator rights are needed. For parallel runs see Parallel runs on Windows.

The Windows builds are older than the Linux one: p1.exe prints Priroda 20 (2021.03.18) and p_190306.exe prints Priroda 19 (2019.03.06). For water the serial p1.exe gave the same energy as Linux version 25 to all printed digits, and the same optimized geometry and frequencies. Features added after version 20 are missing from the Windows builds.

In 2017 users referred to the parallel Windows build as exe64/p.exe. The current index has no p.exe; the newest parallel build there is p_190306.exe.

Old 32-bit Windows builds could not allocate more than about 1 GB of memory; malloc(...) failed appeared above that. The 64-bit p1.exe ran with mem=3000 without trouble.

Running a calculation¶

Serial runs¶

Give the input file first and the output file second:

p input.in output.out

On Windows:

p1.exe input.in output.out

On Linux the current directory is usually not in PATH, so start the program as ./p or with its full path. If the program cannot find the input or the basis file, give full paths everywhere: for the executable, the input, the output, and the basis file inside the input.

Run in a directory you own and can write to. Keep file and directory names to Latin letters, digits and simple punctuation, with no spaces or Cyrillic. This also applies to the computer name on Windows. File names are case-sensitive on Linux, although keywords are not.

The Windows p1.exe (version 20) did run in a folder with a space in its name, both from inside it and from outside with the paths in double quotes. Full Windows paths such as C:\Work\mol.in work for the input and output files.

One user of an older version saw the complaint 0: output file 'tasK.out'? when the output file name contained a capital letter. Version 25 writes to an output file with capital letters in its name without complaint.

If no output file is given (p input.in), the output goes to standard output.

Parallel runs on Linux¶

Priroda is parallelized with MPI. Start a parallel run through an MPI launcher. The official site shows the mpiexec that it ships next to p:

./mpiexec -np 4 ./p input.in output.out

The output then starts with parallel on 4 processors and one node N: line per process. A two-process test gave exactly the serial energy.

Older versions also accepted p -np 4 input.in output.out, which users ran with versions 6 and 10. Version 25 does not: it takes -np as the input file name, prints input file '-np'?. and stops. One site ran version 14 with the bundled mpiexec (mpiexec -np N p input.in, output to standard output).

Check the start of the output. A parallel run prints the number of processes and one line per process:

 parallel on  4 processors
 node  0: 'linux-ldmm'
 node  1: 'linux-ldmm'
 ...

The official site gives one example for a cluster build, p_l under Slurm:

sbatch -p test -n 16 -t 6 impi ~/bin/p_l file.{in,out}

Here impi is presumably that cluster’s Intel MPI wrapper script; it is not part of Priroda.

Parallel runs on Windows, scaling and batch-job scripts are covered in Parallel and cluster runs.

Memory, disk and scratch: $system¶

The $system group sets the resources. Every limit applies per MPI process. disk=10 on four processes can use up to 40 GB.

$system memory=2048 disk=-2048 path=/scratch/user $end
memory

Memory in MB. Two values set rank 0 and the other ranks separately: mem=2048,256 gives the master process 2048 MB and every other process 256 MB. The version 5 documentation says that in a parallel run most of the memory and all of the disk storage are used by rank 0. That is why a small second value works: the other ranks need less.

disk

A positive value is scratch disk in GB. The program opens one scratch file per gigabyte. A negative value is scratch kept in memory, in MB (a RAM disk): disk=-2048 holds 2048 MB of scratch in RAM. A second value applies to the other ranks, as for memory; the official example inputs typically give them -1.

path

The scratch directory. A colon-separated list gives one directory per process, which pays off only when the directories are on different physical drives. For several processes and one fast disk, a single directory is enough.

Keeping scratch in memory¶

With a negative disk, memory plus |disk| is taken by every process, so the sum over all processes must fit into the node’s physical RAM, or the run stops at once with malloc(...) failed. With mem=a,b and disk=a,b, rank 0 takes the first values and every other rank the second. One user’s setting for a 24 GB node is memory=9000 disk=-14000; that fills the node with one process. On several processes, give the other ranks small second values or lower the limits.

Keeping the scratch in RAM is faster than a local disk; one user calls it “a bit faster”. In an older cluster benchmark the gain was larger: a version 8 RI-MP2 job on 8 cores (4 nodes) took 12.4 minutes with scratch in RAM, against 72 minutes on 2 cores with scratch on disk and 86 minutes on 8 cores with direct SCF and scratch on disk.

Where scratch files go¶

The scratch directory is taken from path=, then from the TMPDIR environment variable. The files are named tmp<number>.<suffix>, for example /tmp/tmp2960.0 or /tmp/tmp9633.11. In version 25 each process of a parallel run wrote its own file with a different number and the same suffix (tmp5345.0000, tmp5346.0000). Priroda deletes them at the end of a normal run, and in version 25 also when the job is stopped with signal 15 (SIGTERM). After a crash, delete the leftovers yourself.

When neither path= nor TMPDIR is set, version 25 puts scratch files in /tmp (echo Disk:   1g '/tmp'), as version 6 did. input.txt says the current working directory instead, and a 2020 user report gives the directory of the input file; neither matches version 25. /tmp is often small or shared, so set path= or TMPDIR for real jobs.

On Windows there is no /tmp. Without path= or TMPDIR, the run stops after printing 0: opening file /tmp/tmp978.0000 (the number varies), and the output ends with process 0 got signal 6. This still happens with p1.exe (version 20). Any of these avoids it:

  • $system path=. $end (the current directory);

  • TMPDIR set to a Windows path: in cmd.exe, set TMPDIR=%TEMP% or set "TMPDIR=%TEMP%". Do not write set TMPDIR="%TEMP%": cmd.exe keeps the quotes in the value, Priroda takes the result as a relative path, and the run stops in the same way;

  • a RAM disk (negative disk), which needs no scratch directory. An input with no $system group gets a 512 MB RAM disk and runs.

Disk speed¶

Warning

Never put scratch files on NFS or another network file system. On most clusters the home directories are on NFS; use the node-local scratch disk instead.

Priroda is sensitive to disk speed. The unofficial keyword list input.txt warns that for all methods except GGA DFT, performance “will be degraded terribly” if more than one process reads and writes large files on the same physical drive. In order of preference:

  1. keep the scratch in RAM (negative disk) if it fits;

  2. give each process its own physical drive with path=a:b:c:d;

  3. put all processes on one fast local disk (SSD), accepting some loss.

If the disk is the bottleneck for RI-MP2 or RI-DFT, $integral direct=1 recomputes the integrals instead of storing them. One user found it uses about a third of the memory but runs about ten times longer in CPU time. In a disk-bound RI-MP2 optimization another user got 20 steps overnight with it instead of 2.

Users also recommend more RAM over faster disks. Scratch on a separate SSD helps, but RAM matters more.

When the limits are too small¶

Priroda does not fall back to a slower algorithm when memory or scratch runs out. The run stops with an error such as need … bytes. (the memory limit is too small), malloc(536870912) failed (the machine cannot supply the memory) or, for scratch, 0: out of disk space (grid_W), 8213824 (version 25; older versions printed the number with KB). Raise the limit in $system, move to a node with more resources, or choose a cheaper method (RI-MP2 instead of conventional MP2).

If you omit $system, version 6 printed Memory: 128 (128) MB and Disk: 1 GB '/tmp'. Version 25 prints Memory: 256m + 512m (256m + 512m) and no Disk: line. Read by the echo format, that is 256 MB of memory and a 512 MB RAM disk per process. That is enough for small molecules only, so always give $system for anything larger than a test.

If a run fails for lack of memory or disk, see Memory, disk and scratch errors.

Input file requirements¶

The input is a plain text file. Write it in a plain-text editor, not a word processor.

  • Plain ASCII. Keywords, values and file names should contain ASCII characters only. Do not save the file as Unicode.

  • Unix line endings (LF). This holds on Windows too. Saving from Word as “plain text” still leaves Windows (CRLF) line endings, and some editors need to be told explicitly to write Unix line endings.

  • Straight quotes. Write basis="3z.bas" with the ASCII double quote. Typographic quotes, as in basis=»3z.bas», break the basis-file name.

Users of versions 6–10 reported that an input with CRLF line endings fails in $molecule, because the carriage return becomes part of the keyword. The output stops after a line like this, where the keyword z-matrix or cartesian is shown garbled by the carriage return:

 molecule input: ''
' ?matrix

Variants seen are ?rtesian for cartesian, 'z-matrix' ?, and 'cartesian followed by ' ? on the next line. A less obvious case: an input edited in Word ran task=scan as a plain optimization.

Version 25 behaves the same way: a water input saved with Windows line endings stopped after molecule input: '' with the line 'cartesian' ?, exit status 1. The Windows build p1.exe (version 20) stops in the same place, so the input needs Unix line endings on Windows too.

To check and fix the line endings on Linux:

file mol.in        # reports "with CRLF line terminators" if the file has Windows endings
dos2unix mol.in

Running dos2unix on a file that already has Unix line endings does no harm. On Windows, Notepad++ and the FAR Manager editor (Shift+F2, then UNIX (LF)) can convert line endings.

For the full list of input-reading failures and their symptoms, see The input is not read, or is read wrongly.

Basis-set files¶

The basis sets, their auxiliary (fitting) sets and the ECPs are read from a separate file named by $control basis. The set itself is chosen with set= in $molecule; without it, the default set of the file is used. Without basis=, the basis data are read from the input file itself.

Give the basis file as a full path:

$control task=optimize basis=/home/user/priroda/basis/basis.in $end

In version 25, basis=basis.in works when the file is in the directory you run from, which in the test was also the directory of the input. One user’s parallel run stopped after the node list with application called MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1) - process 0 and worked once the basis file was given with its full path.

  • The name can be put in double quotes: basis="3z.bas" works. Two single quotes do not work; basis=''3z.bas'' fails with error opening file ''3z.bas''.

  • Windows paths work: basis=D:\NMR\Nature\basis\6-31+G(d). In a test, basis=C:\Priroda\basis.in, basis=C:/Priroda/basis.in and basis=basis.in (the file in the directory the run started from) all worked.

  • The relativistic file basis4.in needs four=1 in $control. Without it the basis input fails: in version 25 the output ends right after Basis set input: '…/basis4.in' with the single line 1?.

Which basis files exist and which sets they contain is described with $control basis.
